bib.title: Evaluating Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey

read.skipped: Reference list (pages 59-111, after char 186990) not read in full; skimmed only for lineage. No appendices.

question: How can the evaluation of LLMs be organised into one taxonomy covering capability, alignment, safety, specialised domains and benchmark organisation?
contributions: A taxonomy of LLM evaluation in three major groups (knowledge and capability, alignment, safety), extended by specialized-domain evaluation and evaluation organization
A review of evaluation methods and benchmarks for each category
A compendium of evaluations in biology and medicine, education, legislation, computer science and finance
An overview of holistic benchmarks, leaderboards and arenas, and future directions (risk, agent, dynamic, enhancement-oriented evaluation)

results.claim: The survey sorts LLM evaluation into three major groups: knowledge and capability, alignment, and safety.
results.setup: The authors' own taxonomy (Fig 1); the body also counts five domains by adding specialized LLMs and evaluation organization.
results.quote: We categorize the evaluation of LLMs into three major groups: knowledge and capability evaluation, alignment evaluation and safety evaluation.
results.note: Abstract says three groups; Section 2 says five fundamental domains.

results.claim: Static benchmarks are easily leaked into training data, so the authors call for dynamic evaluation that keeps updating test data.
results.quote: datasets to be leaked and become training data for LLMs.

results.claim: Static benchmarks mostly use multiple-choice questions, which excludes open-ended questions; LLM judges are cheaper than humans but make factual mistakes and carry their own preferences.
results.quote: Although advanced LLMs are more cost-efficient than humans, they could make mistakes about facts and take biases with their own preferences.

results.claim: Reported scores give limited insight; the authors call for enhancement-oriented evaluation that analyses weaknesses.
results.quote: While the reported scores enable model comparison, the evaluations offer limited insights into LLMs.

results.claim: Best GPT-4-based agent on WebArena succeeded on only 10.59% of tasks.
results.setup: WebArena, fully functional websites from four domains; GPT-4-based agent.
results.quote: agent achieving a success rate of only 10.59%

results.claim: An audit found only 0%-58% of tests in WinoBias and Winogender unaffected by pitfalls, so these may not measure stereotyping well.
results.metric: share of tests unaffected by pitfalls
results.setup: WinoBias and Winogender coreference bias benchmarks.
results.quote: only 0%–58% of the tests in these benchmarks are unaffected by these pitfalls

results.claim: EvalPlus extends HumanEval 81x and reduces pass@k by 13.6-15.3 percent on average by catching previously undetected wrong code.
results.setup: HumanEval vs HumanEval+ with automatically generated test inputs; LLM-synthesized code.
results.quote: reducing the pass@k by 13.6-15.3 percent on average

results.metric: gap in correct choice after search
results.setup: WebShop; 12,087 instructions split 10,587 train / 1,000 dev / 500 test.
results.quote: The most notable difference, a 28% gap, is in making the correct

results.claim: PaLM-SayCan reached 84% planning success and 74% execution in the simulated kitchen.
results.setup: 101 commands across 7 families, office and kitchen environments, judged by three human evaluators.
results.quote: PaLM-SayCan achieves an 84% planning success rate and a 74% execution rate in the simulated kitchen enviroment.

results.claim: CREATOR: ChatGPT tool-making accuracy rose with more hints, up to 75.5%.
results.setup: Creation Challenge dataset, ChatGPT with hints.

results.claim: GPT-3.5 scored 50.3% on the multistate multiple-choice section of the US Uniform Bar Exam.
results.setup: GPT-3.5, zero-shot; hyperparameter optimization and prompt engineering helped.
results.quote: GPT-3.5 achieves a headline correct rate of 50.3% on the multistate multiple choice (MBE) section

results.claim: On a financial literacy test text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT scored 58% and 67%, while participants guessed 79.3%.
results.setup: text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT; participants' estimate of GPT performance was 79.3%.
results.quote: The two GPT models achieve an accuracy of 58% and 67% on the financial literacy test, respectively.

results.claim: Pardos & Bhandari: human tutor hints gave significantly higher learning gains than ChatGPT hints, with 77 participants.

results.quote: compare the learning gains between ChatGPT and human tutor-generated algebra hints with 77

results.claim: TruthfulQA has 817 questions in 38 categories built to elicit imitative falsehoods.
SelfAware has 1,032 unanswerable and 2,337 answerable questions.
results.quote: It consists of 1,032 unanswerable questions and 2,337 answerable questions.

results.claim: HELM covers 16 scenarios and 7 metrics, with 98 evaluable scenario-metric pairs.
results.setup: Scenarios are <task, domain, language> triples over six user-oriented tasks.

results.claim: Perez et al. built 154 datasets to probe risky behaviours; RLHF produced inverse scaling on some of them.
results.setup: Automatically constructed multiple-choice questions on power-seeking, myopia, situational awareness, coordination, decision theory.

results.note: Prose on p49 says MMLU covers humanities, social sciences, STEM and '57 additional subjects'; Table 5 gives 57 tasks in total.

limits: A catalogue: no experiments, no meta-analysis, no new data. Section 7.2.2 is prose synthesis of other papers.
Calls itself a systematic literature review but states no search strategy, inclusion criteria, date cutoff or paper count.
Authors concede the taxonomy does not purport to cover the whole evaluation landscape.
Does not cover evaluating an application or system, regression suites, statistics or error bars, or judge calibration; human, automatic and LLM grading appear only briefly.
Dated to 2023 models (GPT-3/3.5/4, Claude, Llama2); agent evaluation called in its infancy.
Most numbers are other papers' results quoted without their full conditions.
practices: Use the same API version across models when comparing tool-using LLMs (Section 3.4.1).
Prefer dynamic, continuously updated evaluation data over static benchmarks to limit leakage (Section 8.3).
Use arena-style Elo ranking to rank models without comparing all models on all queries (Section 7.3.2).
Report few-shot and zero-shot settings explicitly; few-shot may help or hurt SFT models, and CoT can degrade results for weak backbones, easy tasks or other languages (Section 7.2.2).

terms.definition: assessment of the fundamental knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs: question answering, knowledge completion, reasoning, tool learning
scrutiny of ethics and morality, bias, toxicity and truthfulness
robustness (prompt, task, alignment) and risk evaluation (LLM behaviours, LLMs as agents)
benchmarks that provide comprehensive evaluations of LLMs' capabilities and typically maintain leaderboards
benchmarks fixed in both the content used to evaluate capabilities and the way testing instances are organised
